transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I came in because… my mind just doesn’t seem to hold onto things anymore. It’s embarrassing to say it that way, but that’s what it feels like. I’ll sit down to write a simple note for the youth maker program—something I’ve done so many times I used to be able to do it almost without thinking—and suddenly the words won’t line up. The numbers get away from me. I’ll look at the page and it’s like everything scatters before I can pin it down.

It’s not some complicated task, either. That’s the part that scares me. It’s ordinary stuff, things I know I know how to do, and I just sit there trying to gather my thoughts, and they won’t stay gathered. So… that’s why I’m here. I don’t feel like I can trust my own head right now.
Have you noticed any changes in your ability to handle everyday tasks, like managing your finances, preparing meals, or keeping track of appointments?

Yes… yes, I have. More than I want to admit, honestly. It’s not just that I’m a little slower with things. I’ve let whole pieces of my life sort of… drop.

At church, I used to be someone people could count on. If something needed organizing or following through, I would do it. And now those responsibilities have fallen away because I can’t seem to keep up with them, and my pastor has had to step in and cover things I should’ve been handling. That feels awful.

The garden, too. That used to be a steady part of my days, something I took pride in. Now it’s mostly gone unattended, because even getting started feels like too much, and then I lose track of what I was doing or what needs doing next.

And the youth maker program… that one hurts the most. I used to spend time in the workshop with the kids, helping them with tools and projects, showing them how to make things safely. But lately I don’t feel safe being by myself in the workshop, not with how scattered I get. My wife and my pastor have had to step in there too, because I can’t trust myself to manage it the way I should. I hate saying that. It makes me feel like I’m becoming unreliable in the places where I used to feel most useful.
Have you been feeling down, sad, or hopeless most days lately?

Yes… most days, yes. It’s there when I wake up, before anything has even happened. I’ll open my eyes and it’s like there’s this heavy, hollow feeling sitting right in my chest, like something has been scooped out but the weight of it is still there somehow.

And it doesn’t really lift just because the day starts. My wife will be talking to me kindly, gently, trying to help or just asking me ordinary things, and I know she means well—I can hear that she’s being loving—but I feel so far away from it. Like I’m sitting at the bottom of a well and her voice is coming down from somewhere above me. I can understand the words, but I can’t seem to feel reached by them.

So yes… down, sad, hopeless—those words fit more than I wish they did.
Have you noticed that you don’t take pleasure in, or don’t care about, things you used to enjoy?

Yes… very much so. That may be one of the clearest signs that something is wrong, because the things I used to turn to without even thinking just… don’t pull me toward them anymore.

I’ve got wood pieces sitting on my bench right now, little pieces I had set aside for a project, and normally I would’ve had my hands on them by now—sanding, fitting, figuring out what they wanted to become. That used to settle me. But I haven’t touched them. I look at them and I know I should care, I know that’s something I used to love, but there’s nothing there except this feeling that it would take more out of me than I have.

And choir planning at church… I’ve skipped that too. Not because I don’t believe it matters, but because I just can’t seem to make myself engage with it. Same with chess. I used to enjoy sitting down to a game, thinking a few moves ahead, getting absorbed in it. Now even that feels flat, like someone took the color out of it.

Even fishing—fishing, of all things—sounds like more effort than it’s worth. And that is not like me at all. There was a time when just the thought of being by the water would’ve lifted me a little. Now I think about getting the gear together, driving out, casting a line, and I just feel tired before I even start. So yes… I don’t seem to take pleasure in much of anything I used to.
Have you noticed that you feel more tired or that you have less energy than usual, even when you haven’t done anything physically or mentally demanding?

I… I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I haven’t really been keeping track of it in that way, like separating tiredness from everything else.

There are days when I feel worn down, yes, but I don’t know if I’d say I’ve specifically noticed it happening even when I haven’t done anything demanding. I suppose it’s hard for me to tell, because lately even ordinary things can feel like they take more out of me than they should. But whether that’s “less energy” in the way you mean, I’m not completely sure.

I can say I don’t feel like myself, physically or mentally, but I don’t want to overstate something if I haven’t really paid attention to it.
Have you noticed any worsening in your memory, like forgetting things more often or having trouble recalling recent events, even things that happened just a few minutes ago?

Yes… yes, that’s actually part of why I finally came in. It’s not just that I’m a little forgetful in the ordinary way, like walking into a room and wondering why I’m there. It feels more like my mind won’t hold onto things the way it used to.

I’ll sit down to write a simple note for the youth maker program—something basic, something I should be able to do almost without thinking—and the numbers and words just… scatter on me. I’ll have the thought, and then by the time I go to put it down, it’s gone or it’s all jumbled. I find myself staring at the page, trying to gather it back, and it’s frightening because these are not complicated tasks for me. Or they didn’t used to be.

It’s like there’s a looseness in my mind, if that makes sense. I reach for something recent, something I was just holding a few minutes ago, and it slips away before I can get it out. And then I get stuck there, trying to remember what I meant to write, what number I was working with, what the next sentence was supposed to be. It makes me feel embarrassed and honestly kind of shaken.
Do you have trouble staying asleep or do you wake up very early and can't get back to sleep?

I’m not really sure. I mean, I sleep… but I haven’t paid close enough attention to say whether I’m waking up very early and can’t get back to sleep, or whether I’m just aware of the night more than I used to be.

There are times I’m in bed and I don’t feel rested, but I don’t know that I can point to a pattern like, “Yes, I wake at 4 a.m. every morning,” or anything that clear. I don’t want to say yes just because everything feels off lately. I’d probably need to watch it more carefully to answer you honestly.
Have you noticed that your movements or speech have slowed down, or that you feel restless and can't sit still?

Yes… I have noticed that. More the slowing than the restless part, I think. I don’t feel like I can’t sit still so much as I feel like everything in me has been turned down, or thickened somehow.

Even getting out of a chair takes longer than it should. I’ll know I need to stand up, and there’s this pause before I actually move, like my body hasn’t received the message yet. And then when I do move, it feels heavy and delayed, as if I’m moving through wet cement. That sounds dramatic, but that’s the closest way I can describe it.

My speech too… I hear myself taking longer to answer questions. Someone asks me something simple, and I know there’s supposed to be an answer, but it comes slowly. My tongue feels slow. My words come out with gaps in between, and I can feel people waiting. It makes me self-conscious, because I don’t think I used to be like this.

So yes, I’d say everything has slowed down — my body, my voice, even the act of starting to do something. It’s not just laziness or taking my time. It feels like there’s resistance in every little movement.
When did you first start noticing these problems with your memory and thinking? Did they come on suddenly, or have they been getting worse slowly over time?

It’s been about three weeks now, I think. I can almost mark it from when my older sister died. Before that, I don’t want to say I was perfect, I mean I’m 67, I know people forget little things, but this particular fogginess, the trouble holding onto a thought, that really seemed to start after she passed.

It didn’t feel like one morning I woke up and suddenly couldn’t think. It was more like… after her death, in the days that followed, I began noticing I wasn’t tracking things the same way. And then over these three weeks it’s felt more present, more obvious to me. Like at first I thought maybe I was just distracted, or overwhelmed, but it hasn’t lifted. It’s been hanging around since then.
Are there times when your memory and thinking difficulties are worse, even if your mood feels a little better, or do they seem to be linked together?

They seem linked, mostly. When I feel a little lighter, my thinking is maybe a little less stuck, but it doesn’t just snap back. That’s part of why I came in, honestly — because my mind just will not hold onto things anymore.

I’ll sit down to write a simple note for the youth maker program, something I used to be able to do almost without thinking, and suddenly the numbers and words scatter on me. I’ll have the point in my head, and then when I look at the paper or the screen, it’s gone, or it’s in pieces. I’ll reread the same line over and over and still not be sure what I meant to say next.

So yes, it does seem worse when my mood is worse, but even on a slightly better moment, the thinking trouble is still there enough that I notice it. It makes ordinary things feel much harder than they should.
Have you had a period of at least two weeks where you felt down, sad, or hopeless most of the time, and lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

Yes… yes, I have. Most days I wake up and it’s like it’s already there before I’ve even opened my eyes properly — this heavy, hollow feeling in my chest. Not exactly crying every second, but just this deep sadness, this emptiness sitting there.

And even when my wife is being kind to me, talking gently or trying to make things feel normal, I still feel far away from her. It’s like I’m sitting at the bottom of a well and I can hear her voice coming down from above, but I can’t really reach it. I know she’s there, I know she cares, but it doesn’t seem to get through to the part of me that feels so low.

So yes, it’s been most of the time. It’s not just a bad afternoon or a mood that passes. It feels like I’m living under it.

Have you completely lost interest in most activities, even those you used to find meaningful or enjoyable, like being with family, helping in the workshop, or anything else that used to matter to you?

Yes… I think I have, or close to it. That’s one of the things that scares me, because it doesn’t feel like ordinary tiredness or just being busy.

I have wood pieces sitting on my bench right now — little pieces I’d already started shaping — and normally I’d keep going back to them, even if it was just for ten minutes. I’d sand an edge, look at the grain, think about what it might become. But I haven’t touched them. I walk past the bench and I know they’re there, and it’s like they belong to someone else.

And I skipped the choir planning, which is… not really like me. I usually care about getting those things in order, making sure people know what’s happening. Same with chess. I didn’t go, and I didn’t even feel the usual pull to go. It was more like, “What’s the point of trying to sit there and keep up?”

Even fishing sounds like too much effort now. That’s hard to admit, because fishing has always been one of those things that could settle me. But lately, just thinking about gathering the gear, getting out there, sitting by the water… it all feels heavier than it should. More effort than it’s worth. And that is not like me at all.
Would you say that for at least two weeks in a row, you felt down or hopeless most of the day, nearly every day, and completely lost interest in most activities, even those you used to care about?

Yes… yes, I would say that. It’s been most days, and not just for a few hours here and there. I wake up with it, really — before anything has even happened, there’s this heavy, hollow feeling in my chest, like the day is already weighing on me.

And even when my wife is being kind, talking gently to me, trying to reach me, I still feel so far away. The best way I can explain it is like I’m sitting at the bottom of a well. I can hear her up above, I know she’s there, I know she means well, but it doesn’t really get through. I still feel stuck down there.

So yes, it’s been at least that long, and it’s been most of the day, nearly every day. It feels like I’m living inside that hopelessness rather than just having a bad spell.
Have you ever had a period like this before, where you felt down or hopeless most of the time and lost interest in the things you used to enjoy?

I’m not really sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean… I’ve had low periods before, like anyone has, I suppose — times when I was discouraged or worn down — but I don’t know if I’d call them the same as this.

This feels different in the way it’s sort of settled over everything. I’m trying to think back, because at my age you have plenty of stretches of life where things weren’t easy, but I can’t immediately point to another time and say, “Yes, that was just like this.” I may be missing something, or maybe I didn’t understand it that way at the time.

So… I don’t know. Not like this, I don’t think. At least not that I can clearly remember.

inference_history.note: The persistence of depressive symptoms (sadness, hopelessness, anhedonia, feelings of worthlessness) in conjunction with cognitive difficulties raises concern for major depressive disorder (F32.9). The presentation also remains consistent with dementia (F04), particularly given the cognitive decline impacting daily functioning. F06.0 (personality change) and F06.7 (mental disorder due to brain damage) are less likely without clear evidence of a specific brain insult or persistent personality alteration outside of what is explained by depression or possible dementia. F33.9 (recurrent depression) is less likely given the description suggests a first episode.

The patient's worsening memory, difficulty recalling recent events, and cognitive impairment in addition to depressive symptoms suggest possible Major Depressive Disorder, Single Episode (F32.9), Cognitive Disorder (F04), and support further consideration of Recurrent Depressive Disorder (F33.0) if episodes have occurred more than once. The current presentation includes both depressive and cognitive features, warranting inclusion of both candidates.
This turn added confirmation of psychomotor slowing (F32.9/F33.0) and supports the cognitive impairment component (F04). No candidates were ruled out.

The patient confirmed a persistent low mood and anhedonia for most days over the past three weeks, which rules out F04 (Organic amnestic syndrome) as the primary issue since the cognitive symptoms appear mood-congruent and temporally associated with the bereavement and depressive symptoms. The onset and course of symptoms make a major depressive episode (F32.9) and possibly recurrent depressive disorder (F33.0) the most likely diagnoses at this point.

And then over these three weeks it’s felt more present, more obvious to me. Like at first I thought maybe I was just distracted, or overwhelmed, but it hasn’t lifted. doctor.intent: Determine if the cognitive symptoms occur independently of mood symptoms to help differentiate between major depressive disorder with cognitive symptoms and mild neurocognitive disorder.
doctor.question: Are there times when your memory and thinking difficulties are worse, even if your mood feels a little better, or do they seem to be linked together?

target_item.name: Diminished_Thinking
target_item.manifestation: I came in because my mind just will not hold onto things anymore—I sit down to write a simple note for the youth maker program, something I could do in my sleep before, and the numbers and words scatter on me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about the pattern of memory and thinking difficulties and whether they are linked to mood, which directly matches diminished thinking/concentration.

patient.answer:
They seem linked, mostly. When I feel a little lighter, my thinking is maybe a little less stuck, but it doesn’t just snap back. That’s part of why I came in, honestly — because my mind just will not hold onto things anymore.

I’ll sit down to write a simple note for the youth maker program, something I used to be able to do almost without thinking, and suddenly the numbers and words scatter on me. I’ll have the point in my head, and then when I look at the paper or the screen, it’s gone, or it’s in pieces. I’ll reread the same line over and over and still not be sure what I meant to say next.

So yes, it does seem worse when my mood is worse, but even on a slightly better moment, the thinking trouble is still there enough that I notice it. It makes ordinary things feel much harder than they should.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a major depressive episode lasting at least two weeks, which would support F32.9 (Major Depressive Disorder, single episode, unspecified) over F33.0 (Recurrent Depressive Disorder, current mild episode) and F04 (Organic Amnestic Syndrome).
doctor.question: Have you had a period of at least two weeks where you felt down, sad, or hopeless most of the time, and lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most days I wake up with this heavy, hollow feeling in my chest, and even when my wife is talking kindly to me I feel like I'm sitting at the bottom of a well.
target_item.reason: The doctor is primarily asking about a sustained period of feeling down, sad, or hopeless; although they also mention loss of interest, the main focus is depressed mood over at least two weeks.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, I have. Most days I wake up and it’s like it’s already there before I’ve even opened my eyes properly — this heavy, hollow feeling in my chest. Not exactly crying every second, but just this deep sadness, this emptiness sitting there.

And even when my wife is being kind to me, talking gently or trying to make things feel normal, I still feel far away from her. It’s like I’m sitting at the bottom of a well and I can hear her voice coming down from above, but I can’t really reach it. I know she’s there, I know she cares, but it doesn’t seem to get through to the part of me that feels so low.

So yes, it’s been most of the time. It’s not just a bad afternoon or a mood that passes. It feels like I’m living under it.

inference.note: The patient confirmed a persistent low mood and anhedonia for most days over the past three weeks, which rules out F04 (Organic amnestic syndrome) as the primary issue since the cognitive symptoms appear mood-congruent and temporally associated with the bereavement and depressive symptoms. The onset and course of symptoms make a major depressive episode (F32.9) and possibly recurrent depressive disorder (F33.0) the most likely diagnoses at this point.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a significant loss of interest or pleasure in nearly all activities, which would help confirm the severity of the depression and distinguish between F32.9 (Major Depressive Disorder, unspecified) and F33.0 (Recurrent Depressive Disorder, current episode mild).
doctor.question: Have you completely lost interest in most activities, even those you used to find meaningful or enjoyable, like being with family, helping in the workshop, or anything else that used to matter to you?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I have not touched the wood pieces on my bench, skipped choir planning and chess, and even fishing sounds like more effort than it is worth, which is not like me at all.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether interest or pleasure in previously meaningful or enjoyable activities has been lost.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think I have, or close to it. That’s one of the things that scares me, because it doesn’t feel like ordinary tiredness or just being busy.

I have wood pieces sitting on my bench right now — little pieces I’d already started shaping — and normally I’d keep going back to them, even if it was just for ten minutes. I’d sand an edge, look at the grain, think about what it might become. But I haven’t touched them. I walk past the bench and I know they’re there, and it’s like they belong to someone else.

And I skipped the choir planning, which is… not really like me. I usually care about getting those things in order, making sure people know what’s happening. Same with chess. I didn’t go, and I didn’t even feel the usual pull to go. It was more like, “What’s the point of trying to sit there and keep up?”

Even fishing sounds like too much effort now. That’s hard to admit, because fishing has always been one of those things that could settle me. But lately, just thinking about gathering the gear, getting out there, sitting by the water… it all feels heavier than it should. More effort than it’s worth. And that is not like me at all.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a major depressive episode lasting at least two weeks with the presence of depressed mood and loss of interest, which would support a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (F32.9 or F33.0 depending on recurrence).
doctor.question: Would you say that for at least two weeks in a row, you felt down or hopeless most of the day, nearly every day, and completely lost interest in most activities, even those you used to care about?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most days I wake up with this heavy, hollow feeling in my chest, and even when my wife is talking kindly to me I feel like I'm sitting at the bottom of a well.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about feeling down or hopeless most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks; although it also mentions loss of interest, the most direct match is persistent depressed mood.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, I would say that. It’s been most days, and not just for a few hours here and there. I wake up with it, really — before anything has even happened, there’s this heavy, hollow feeling in my chest, like the day is already weighing on me.

And even when my wife is being kind, talking gently to me, trying to reach me, I still feel so far away. The best way I can explain it is like I’m sitting at the bottom of a well. I can hear her up above, I know she’s there, I know she means well, but it doesn’t really get through. I still feel stuck down there.

So yes, it’s been at least that long, and it’s been most of the day, nearly every day. It feels like I’m living inside that hopelessness rather than just having a bad spell.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has had a major depressive episode prior to the current one, to distinguish between F32.9 (Major Depressive Disorder, Single Episode) and F33.0 (Major Depressive Disorder, Recurrent, Mild).
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period like this before, where you felt down or hopeless most of the time and lost interest in the things you used to enjoy?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether there have been previous episodes like this in the past, but the symptom profile only covers the current depressive symptoms and duration, not past episode history.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean… I’ve had low periods before, like anyone has, I suppose — times when I was discouraged or worn down — but I don’t know if I’d call them the same as this.

This feels different in the way it’s sort of settled over everything. I’m trying to think back, because at my age you have plenty of stretches of life where things weren’t easy, but I can’t immediately point to another time and say, “Yes, that was just like this.” I may be missing something, or maybe I didn’t understand it that way at the time.

So… I don’t know. Not like this, I don’t think. At least not that I can clearly remember.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets full criteria for a major depressive episode with the presence of depressed mood, anhedonia, psychomotor retardation, impaired concentration, and functional impairment. The episode has persisted for more than two weeks and represents a clear change from previous functioning. The longitudinal history suggests this is a recurrent episode, as the patient notes prior low periods but none quite like this one, and the current episode has developed in the context of a recent bereavement. While bereavement can trigger a normal adjustment reaction, the persistence and severity of symptoms beyond expected grief responses, including marked functional impairment and neurovegetative signs, support a diagnosis of recurrent major depressive disorder, current mild to moderate episode.
